The image shows a very young soybean seedling at cotyledon stage emerging from wet, muddy soil. Next to it is a collapsed/failing seedling. Key observations:
- Very wet, saturated soil
- Seedling at early emergence stage
- Adjacent seedling appears rotted/collapsed
- Soft, water-soaked appearance on the failing plant

Top candidates: **Pythium_damping_off**, **Phytophthora**, **Rhizoctonia**

Let me view reference images for these candidates.

The Pythium reference collage is a near-perfect match to the test image — same wet dark soil, same cotyledon stage, same soft seedling collapse. Phytophthora shows older plants with stem discoloration, not early seedling soft rot. Rhizoctonia shows dry, reddish-brown cankers, not soft wet rot.

Let me view 3 more references to fulfill the minimum requirement.

Fusarium shows older root rot, Anthracnose shows mature stem/pod lesions, SDS shows interveinal necrosis on mature leaves. None match the test image.

**Initial prediction: Pythium_damping_off**

The test image shows a cotyledon-stage seedling in very wet, muddy soil with a collapsed adjacent seedling showing soft rot — exactly matching Pythium damping off. Now checking the Attractor Guide.

Pythium_damping_off is not listed as an over-predicted class in the guide, so no alternatives to check. My prediction stands.

**Summary of evidence:**
- Wet, saturated dark soil — classic Pythium-favorable conditions
- Cotyledon-stage seedling at/just after emergence — consistent with post-emergence damping off
- Adjacent collapsed/rotted seedling showing soft water-soaked rot, not dry or firm cankers (rules out Rhizoctonia)
- No brown stem discoloration extending up the stem (rules out Phytophthora)
- Pythium reference collage is a near-identical visual match — same soil, same stage, same soft seedling collapse

Reference collage is a near-identical match. Wet conditions, soft rot (not dry/firm cankers of Rhizoctonia), and lack of upward stem discoloration (rules out Phytophthora) all point strongly to Pythium."}
